solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Re "V", this may upset on horse?

definitions.text: Re "V", this may upset on horse?

indicators.note: upset means knocked over and thrown into disorder, so the letters before it are jumbled

parts.note: H is slang for heroin, which is also called horse

explanation.surface: A puzzled note about a gesture that might cause offence when made from the saddle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' jumbles RE, V and THIS MAY, with H added. In 1971 the showjumper Harvey Smith made a two-fingered V-sign at the judges from his horse, and his name became British slang for that rude gesture.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue describes the rude two-fingered gesture made from horseback, which British slang names after the showjumper.

clue.text: Deacon and subdeacon would typically celebrate this heavenly body?

definitions.text: Deacon and subdeacon would typically celebrate this

parts.note: high means up in the heavens, lofty
a mass is a body of matter

explanation.surface: Church officials at a service, then a teasing aside that the service might be an astronomical object.
explanation.walkthrough: The closing 'heavenly body?' reads as a star or planet; it is wordplay, with heavenly meaning lofty. A High Mass is the solemn sung form of the Catholic Mass.
explanation.definitionFit: A sung Mass with deacon and subdeacon assisting the priest is the traditional solemn form of Catholic worship.

clue.text: Reluctant to communicate quote about cutting revenue

indicators.note: the reversed quote cuts into the revenue word, splitting it open

parts.note: rent is revenue from property

indicators.note: about here means turned round, so the quote word is read backwards

parts.note: to cite is to quote

explanation.surface: Someone tight-lipped when asked to comment on a cut in income.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' looks like it means C (circa) or RE, but here it only turns the quote round; 'cutting' then sets that inside the revenue.
explanation.definitionFit: A reticent person is reserved and holds back from speaking, a direct synonym.

clue.text: That was a standard release from duty

parts.note: ex means former, what something was
a means one
a rate is a standard, as in a first-rate job

explanation.surface: Someone remarking that being let off work was quite normal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That was' reads as part of a sentence but gives EX, as in ex-wife.
explanation.definitionFit: To exonerate can mean to free someone from an obligation or task, as well as to clear of blame.

clue.text: Short of 12 special co-workers, stole fabric — which means, …

parts.note: a team is a group working together
a boa is a long scarf, a kind of stole
twill is a woven fabric with diagonal ribs
i.e. (id est) means 'that is', which means

explanation.surface: A long, broken sentence about stolen fabric and colleagues, which runs on into the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: 12 is MICKEY MOUSE; a 'short' is a short film, and the 1928 cartoon Steamboat Willie made Mickey famous. 'stole' looks like a verb but is the scarf.
explanation.definitionFit: Steamboat Willie is the 1928 Disney cartoon short that introduced Mickey Mouse to cinema audiences.

clue.text: … likely this would end in short supply

indicators.note: supply here is the adjective, more supple, so the words before it bend into a new order

explanation.surface: Continuing 4: a forecast that something will run out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'supply' looks like a noun, as in short supply, but it is the comparative of supple, signalling that WOULD END IN SHORT are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a conversational way of saying something is probable, so it stands in for likely after 'which means'.

clue.text: A lot of people put in rush orders

indicators.note: the answer is put in, sitting inside, the words that follow

explanation.surface: Many customers placing urgent orders.
explanation.definitionFit: A horde is a large crowd or throng of people.

clue.text: Pistol, a form of protection, has gone off

parts.note: johnny is British slang for a condom
food that has gone off is rotten

explanation.surface: A firearm, kept for self-defence, has accidentally fired.
explanation.walkthrough: Pistol is a member of the Sex Pistols, the 1970s punk band whose singer was Johnny Rotten; 'gone off' suggests a gun firing.
explanation.definitionFit: Johnny Rotten was the lead singer of the Sex Pistols, so he is one Pistol.

clue.text: See 7
Bands regularly arranged throughout very large moulding

indicators.note: throughout means spread through the bands, so the second letter also goes inside
the letters for very and large are set at regular intervals among the bands

parts.note: an O is a ring or band, three of them here

explanation.surface: A description of an enormous decorative strip with stripes spaced along it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly arranged throughout' spaces V and L evenly between three Os.
explanation.definitionFit: An ovolo is a convex architectural moulding, roughly a quarter-circle in section.

clue.text: Reach grand number — party!

parts.note: to reach a place is to get to it
G is slang for a grand, a thousand
ether is something that numbs, an anaesthetic

explanation.surface: A cheer at hitting a big total, then let's celebrate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'number' is not a figure but something that numbs: ether, the old anaesthetic.
explanation.definitionFit: A get-together is an informal social gathering, a party.

clue.text: Become very angry, not getting one's jam and cream cake

indicators.note: not getting means doing without, so these letters are removed

parts.note: to do one's nut is British slang for losing one's temper
the letters of one's are taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone furious at missing out on their filled pastry.
explanation.walkthrough: DO ONE'S NUT is British slang for flying into a rage; 'not getting one's' takes out ONES.
explanation.definitionFit: A doughnut, often spelt donut, is a fried cake commonly filled with jam and cream.

clue.text: Mortimer, his original name, inferior?

definitions.meaning: Walt Disney first called his mouse character Mortimer before renaming him
... as an adjective means trivial or second-rate

explanation.surface: A note about someone's first name, followed by a slight on their worth.
explanation.definitionFit: Disney's cartoon star was first named Mortimer Mouse, and the phrase is also slang for shoddy or amateurish.

clue.text: Longing for a bit of old Tokyo?

definitions.meaning: a Japanese coin, a piece of Tokyo money

explanation.surface: Nostalgia for a fragment of the historic Japanese capital.
explanation.definitionFit: A yen is both a strong desire and the Japanese currency unit.

clue.text: This'll rouse snoozers — and I don't play it down!

indicators.note: to rouse is to stir up, so the letters are stirred into a new order

explanation.surface: A musician boasting that their loud playing will wake sleepers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rouse' looks like waking people but stirs SNOOZERS AND I into a new order.
explanation.definitionFit: This Italian musical direction means 'without mute', so the player does not soften the sound.

clue.text: Comparatively speaking, the right change?

parts.note: an old British simile compares being right to a small pre-decimal sum of money, so the right change is that sum

explanation.surface: A question about whether one was given correct change.
explanation.walkthrough: 'As right as ninepence' is an old British phrase meaning in perfect order; ninepence was a sum in pre-decimal coinage.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom compares rightness to this old sum of money, so it is the 'right' amount of change.

clue.text: Arrangement of Rossini with William Tell's most common cuts

indicators.note: an arrangement in music reworks a piece, here reordering the letters

parts.note: L appears four times in WILLIAM TELL, more than any other letter

explanation.surface: A version of the composer's work alongside his famous overture's best-known passages.
explanation.walkthrough: 'William Tell's most common' is not a tune but its commonest letter, L, which joins ROSSINI in the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: Sirloins are prime cuts of beef from the loin.

clue.text: Works like installing alternative to electric oven

indicators.note: installing means fitting inside, so the like-word takes in the rest

parts.note: as means like
gas is the usual alternative to electric power for cooking
an Aga is a British brand of cast-iron range cooker

explanation.surface: A kitchen fitter's note on putting in a gas cooker instead of an electric one.
explanation.walkthrough: An Aga is a heavy range cooker found in British country kitchens; Aga sagas are novels about comfortable rural middle-class life.
explanation.definitionFit: Aga sagas are a genre of fiction, so they are literary works.

clue.text: An ovation, then, from Starmer & co, utterly outclassed?

indicators.note: from places the source first, so the Labour word comes before the ovation

parts.note: Keir Starmer led the Labour Party, the political left
a standing ovation, so standing is the kind of ovation

explanation.surface: The Labour benches applaud, though they have been beaten badly.
explanation.walkthrough: Keir Starmer leads Britain's Labour Party, so he and colleagues are the LEFT.
explanation.definitionFit: To leave someone standing is to outpace them easily, so a rival left standing has been completely outclassed.

clue.text: Having capacity of two pints, right out of it!

indicators.note: out of it means removed from the word just named

parts.note: a quart is two pints

explanation.surface: A container holding a quart, and someone who has drunk it all and is out of it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out of it' suggests drunkenness but tells you to take RT out of QUART.
explanation.definitionFit: Qua is Latin-derived and means 'in the capacity or role of'.

clue.text: Palace gives us chance we squander needing to net a second

indicators.note: chance as in by chance: random, so the letters fall in a haphazard order

explanation.surface: The Palace offers an opportunity that we waste unless we catch a moment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'chance' rearranges WE SQUANDER, and 'needing to net' has it take in A and S, which end up split apart, so all twelve letters are best seen as one pool. The Queen's Awards for Enterprise were UK business honours conferred by the monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: Queen's Awards were honours presented by the monarch from Buckingham Palace, so they are what the Palace gives.

clue.text: See 19
Dad facing troubles, one of his boys adopted financial deterrents

indicators.note: facing means in front of, so the dad word comes before the troubles
adopting takes something in, so the father word takes in the boy

parts.note: pop is an informal word for father
I is the Roman numeral one
a son is one of a father's boys
ills are troubles

explanation.surface: A father beset by problems, one of whose sons was adopted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'adopted' looks like a family fact but is the container signal; 'facing' puts the dad before the troubles. A poison pill makes a company costly to take over.
explanation.definitionFit: A poison pill is a tactic a company uses to deter a hostile takeover.

clue.text: Diarist's entourage detected in the auditorium

indicators.note: an auditorium is where things are heard, so this tells you the word is said aloud

parts.note: peeps is slang for one's people, an entourage

explanation.surface: A writer's retinue spotted in a theatre audience.
explanation.walkthrough: Samuel Pepys, the 17th-century London diarist, is pronounced 'peeps'.
explanation.definitionFit: Samuel Pepys is England's most famous diarist, so he is the diarist named.

clue.text: Wipe over the contents of one's area

indicators.note: over means turned over, so the hidden letters read backwards
the contents of the words are the letters held inside them

explanation.surface: An instruction to clean whatever fills your patch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the contents of' finds the letters inside ONE'S AREA, and 'over' reads them backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: To erase is to wipe away, as a recording or a board is wiped clean.

clue.text: Something Trump's created? Nice lad involved in this provocative act

indicators.note: in places the shuffled lad inside the smell word

parts.note: to trump is British slang for breaking wind, which creates a pong, a bad smell

indicators.note: involved means tangled up, so these letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A jibe at a politician's doings, then a nice young man mixed up in a racy performance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trump' is not the politician: trump is British slang for a fart, so what it creates is a PONG, a smell; 'involved' jumbles NICE LAD inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Pole dancing is a sexually suggestive dance performed around a vertical pole.

clue.text: Children's character looking out of place in the Big Apple

indicators.note: in means placed inside, so the odd word goes into the city abbreviation

parts.note: the Big Apple is New York, NY
something odd looks out of place

explanation.surface: A storybook figure who seems lost in Manhattan.
explanation.walkthrough: Noddy is a toy-town figure from Enid Blyton's British children's books.
explanation.definitionFit: Noddy is a much-loved character from Enid Blyton's stories for young children.

clue.text: Visionary women at intervals receiving tips from hang-gliders near steep cliffs?

indicators.note: at intervals means the two received tips are not kept together but sit apart in the word
receiving means taking in, so the visionary women's word holds the tips

parts.note: seeresses are female seers, women with visions

indicators.note: tips are the leading letters of the words that follow

explanation.surface: Prophetesses watching hang-gliders launch near a precipice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'receiving at intervals' places H and N at two separate points in SEERESSES. Sheernesses, abrupt steepnesses, is a playful plural for cliffs.
explanation.definitionFit: Sheerness is steepness, so cliffs are examples of sheernesses, hence the question mark.
